summary: A 1980 specification of the DoD standard Transmission Control Protocol, an early form of TCP for reliable data streams. It was replaced by RFC 793 and RFC 7805, and it is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: Sending a long letter in numbered pieces so nothing is missing. This was an early version of that idea.

subtitle: An early specification of the Transmission Control Protocol for reliable data streams

tldr.problem: In 1980, the military and government networks needed a standard protocol that could reliably send data across unreliable, interconnected packet-switched networks with different security and precedence levels.
tldr.mechanism: The TCP provides a connection-oriented, end-to-end reliable delivery service. It breaks data into segments with sequence numbers, acknowledges receipt, retransmits lost data, and uses a three-way handshake to establish connections safely.
tldr.outcome: RFC 761 was replaced by RFC 793 and RFC 7805 (now Historic). This DoD standard became the foundation for TCP and remains central to modern Internet communication.

today: RFC 761 is Historic, replaced by RFC 793 and RFC 7805. It represents the 1980 DoD standard TCP specification and remains a key reference for understanding TCP's design.

sections.title: What TCP Does
sections.content:
The Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) is a host-to-host protocol for reliable communication between processes on different computers in interconnected networks. It assumes the lower-level Internet Protocol will deliver datagrams, but those datagrams may be lost, delayed, duplicated, or reordered. TCP's job is to make the communication reliable and ordered.

TCP sits above the Internet Protocol and below application protocols like Telnet and file transfer. It provides a connection-oriented service: processes establish a connection, exchange data in both directions at once (full duplex), and close the connection when done.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP makes sure that when you send a message across the Internet, it gets there in the right order and nothing is lost.

sections.title: The TCP Segment Header
sections.content: Every TCP segment starts with a header that identifies the source and destination ports (16 bits each), the sequence number of the first data byte (32 bits), and the acknowledgment number indicating the next expected sequence number (32 bits). Control bits (SYN, ACK, FIN, RST, URG, and EOL) signal connection state changes, data acknowledgment, and urgent data. A 16-bit window field tells the sender how much more data the receiver can accept. A checksum covers the header, data, and a pseudo-header from the IP layer to catch transmission errors and misrouted segments.
sections.plainLanguage: Each chunk sent has a label saying where it came from, where it is going, what number it is, what number you are expecting next, and a check digit.

sections.title: Establishing and Closing Connections
sections.content: Processes create sockets by combining an IP address and a port number. A pair of sockets uniquely identifies a connection. To establish a connection safely, TCP uses a three-way handshake with sequence number synchronization: the client sends a SYN segment with its initial sequence number, the server replies with a SYN-ACK acknowledging that number and sending its own, and the client sends an ACK. This guards against erroneous or replay attacks. To close a connection, either side sends a FIN segment, and the other side acknowledges and closes.
sections.plainLanguage: Before sending real data, both sides send SYN messages to agree on starting numbers so they can track each chunk.

sections.title: Reliability and Flow Control
sections.content: TCP assigns a sequence number to each octet sent. The receiver acknowledges receipt and tells the sender how much buffer space it has (the window). If an acknowledgment does not arrive within a timeout, TCP retransmits. At the receiver, sequence numbers are used to discard duplicates and reorder out-of-order segments. A checksum catches damaged segments, which are discarded. The sender also marks end-of-letter boundaries so the receiving process knows where records end. Precedence and security information from the IP layer is carried end-to-end.
sections.plainLanguage: If a chunk does not arrive, you send it again. The other side checks for damage and puts everything in the right order.

fields.name: Sequence Number
fields.desc: Sequence number of the first data octet in this segment.

fields.name: Acknowledgment Number
fields.desc: The next sequence number expected by the sender of this segment.

fields.name: Data Offset
fields.desc: Number of 32-bit words in the TCP header.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Reserved for future use, must be zero.

fields.name: Window
fields.desc: Octets the sender is willing to accept.

fields.name: Urgent Pointer
fields.desc: Offset of urgent data from sequence number.
